# Exercise 9.1 — Variable importance, and a column of pure noise {#sec-importance}

Day 5 ended with a random forest that predicts diabetes well but cannot be
read like a tree or a logistic regression. The first question everyone asks of
such a model is: **which variables does it use?** This exercise answers it in
two ways, and then tests both with a column we know to be useless.

::: {.callout-note}
## The plots are for looking at
The code for every plot is folded away just above it, in case you are curious,
and all of it is in the notebook linked at the top of each tab. You are not
expected to write it yourself.
:::

### Packages and data

```{r}
# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, remove the # and run this line once:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels", "ranger", "vip"))

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(vip)                   # variable importance for many kinds of model

theme_set(theme_bw())          # white background for every plot
options(pillar.sigfig = 3)     # show three significant figures in tables
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 1 — The forest

The same 750 people and five predictors as Day 5, from
[`data/diabetes_clean.csv`](data/diabetes_clean.csv): number of pregnancies,
glucose, BMI (`mass`), the diabetes pedigree function and age. As always, 80%
of the people are used for training and 20% are held back as the test set.

```{r}
diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv") |>
  select(pregnant, glucose, mass, pedigree, age, diabetes) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

set.seed(42)
split <- initial_split(diabetes, prop = 0.8)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)
```

A random forest of 500 trees, as on Day 5. `importance = "impurity"` asks
ranger to keep a record of how much each variable helped while it grows the
trees; Part 2 reads it. A forest is random, so set the seed first.

```{r}
rf_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity") |>
  set_mode("classification")

set.seed(1)
rf_fit <- rf_spec |> fit(diabetes ~ ., data = train)

test_preds <- test |>
  bind_cols(predict(rf_fit, new_data = test, type = "prob"),
            predict(rf_fit, new_data = test))

roc_auc(test_preds, truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second")
```

The test AUC is 0.753. This is the model we explain all day. Python grows
different random trees, so its numbers differ slightly.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 2 — Impurity importance

**Impurity importance** adds up, for each variable, how much purer its splits
made the training rows, over all the trees. The forest works it out while it
is fitted, so it is free. `vi()` from the **vip** package reads it.
ranger reports a raw total; divide by the sum to get each variable's share.

```{r}
vi(rf_fit) |>
  mutate(share = Importance / sum(Importance))
```

Glucose has 0.373 of the total, then BMI 0.182, age 0.164, pedigree 0.162
and pregnancies 0.119. Glucose comes first by a long way.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 3 — Permutation importance

**Permutation importance** asks a different question: *how much worse is the
model on the test rows if one variable is scrambled?* Shuffle one column so
its values land on the wrong people, predict again, and see how much the AUC
drops. The model is not refitted.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
set.seed(1)
test_shuffled <- test |>
  mutate(glucose = sample(______))               # glucose now belongs to someone else

test_shuffled |>
  bind_cols(predict(rf_fit, new_data = ______, type = "prob")) |>
  roc_auc(truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second")
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
`sample(glucose)` returns the same glucose values in a random order. Then
predict on the shuffled test rows, `test_shuffled`.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
set.seed(1)
test_shuffled <- test |>
  mutate(glucose = sample(glucose))

test_shuffled |>
  bind_cols(predict(rf_fit, new_data = test_shuffled, type = "prob")) |>
  roc_auc(truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second")
```

With glucose shuffled the AUC falls from 0.753 to 0.578, a drop of 0.175.
Run it with another seed and the drop changes a little.
:::
:::

One shuffle is one random draw, so in Part 4 we repeat it 20 times for each
variable and take the average drop.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 4 — A control: a column of pure noise

Which measure should we believe? Test both on something whose answer we
already know: [`data/diabetes_noise.csv`](data/diabetes_noise.csv) is the same
file with one more column, `noise`: random numbers unrelated to anything. Its
true importance is **zero**.

Read it, keep `noise` as a sixth predictor, and split it exactly as before.
The same seed gives the same people in the test set.

```{r}
diabetes_noise <- read_csv("data/diabetes_noise.csv") |>
  select(pregnant, glucose, mass, pedigree, age, noise, diabetes) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

set.seed(42)
split_noise <- initial_split(diabetes_noise, prop = 0.8)
train_noise <- training(split_noise)
test_noise  <- testing(split_noise)
```

Fit the same forest on these training rows and look at its impurity
importance.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
set.seed(1)
rf_noise <- rf_spec |> fit(diabetes ~ ., data = ______)

vi(rf_noise) |>
  mutate(share = Importance / sum(Importance))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
Use the training rows that contain the new column, `train_noise`. The formula
`diabetes ~ .` picks up `noise` by itself.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
set.seed(1)
rf_noise <- rf_spec |> fit(diabetes ~ ., data = train_noise)

vi(rf_noise) |>
  mutate(share = Importance / sum(Importance))
```

`noise` gets 0.130 of the total, fourth of six: ahead of the pedigree
function (0.127) and pregnancies (0.109). By this measure, random numbers are
a respectable predictor.
:::
:::

Now the permutation importance of the same forest on the test rows. The loop
does what you did in Part 3, 20 times for each of the six variables. Read it
line by line; it takes a few seconds.

```{r}
auc_before <- test_noise |>
  bind_cols(predict(rf_noise, new_data = test_noise, type = "prob")) |>
  roc_auc(truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second") |>
  pull(.estimate)

set.seed(1)
perm_results <- data.frame()                          # one row per shuffle

for (variable in c("pregnant", "glucose", "mass", "pedigree", "age", "noise")) {
  for (repeat_number in 1:20) {
    test_shuffled <- test_noise
    test_shuffled[[variable]] <- sample(test_shuffled[[variable]])

    auc_after <- test_shuffled |>
      bind_cols(predict(rf_noise, new_data = test_shuffled, type = "prob")) |>
      roc_auc(truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second") |>
      pull(.estimate)

    perm_results <- bind_rows(perm_results,
                              data.frame(variable = variable,
                                         auc_drop = auc_before - auc_after))
  }
}

perm_importance <- perm_results |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  summarise(importance = mean(auc_drop), sd = sd(auc_drop)) |>
  arrange(desc(importance))

perm_importance
```

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
perm_importance |>
  ggplot(aes(x = importance, y = reorder(variable, importance))) +
  geom_col(fill = "coral") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = importance - sd, xmax = importance + sd),
                width = 0.3, orientation = "y") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  labs(x = "Mean drop in test AUC when the variable is shuffled (± 1 SD)",
       y = NULL, title = "Random forest: permutation importance")
```

`noise` comes out at 0.0004, with a standard deviation of 0.009: zero, as it
should. Only glucose (0.129) and BMI (0.028) clearly beat it. The pedigree
function (0.011) is within about one standard deviation of it, and age and
pregnancies come out slightly *below* it: the forest predicts new people no
better with them than without.

Why the difference? Deep trees always find *some* split on a column with many
different values that tidies up a few training rows. Impurity importance
counts that; permutation importance on new people does not. So a variable that
does not clearly beat `noise` should not be called important.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key points
- Impurity importance is free and quick, but it is computed on the training rows and is biased: it gave pure noise 13% of the total.
- Permutation importance is the drop in test AUC when one column is shuffled. Repeat the shuffle and report the mean and spread.
- A noise column is a control: its true importance is zero, and permutation importance puts it there.
:::

### Packages and data

```{python}
# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, install it once from a terminal
# (in a Jupyter notebook, type %pip instead of pip):
# pip install pandas numpy matplotlib scikit-learn

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 1 — The forest

The same 750 people and five predictors as Day 5, from
[`data/diabetes_clean.csv`](data/diabetes_clean.csv): number of pregnancies,
glucose, BMI (`mass`), the diabetes pedigree function and age. As always, 80%
of the people are used for training and 20% are held back as the test set.

```{python}
diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv")
diabetes = diabetes[["pregnant", "glucose", "mass", "pedigree", "age", "diabetes"]]
diabetes["diabetes"] = (diabetes["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)       # 1 = pos, 0 = neg

predictors = ["pregnant", "glucose", "mass", "pedigree", "age"]

train, test = train_test_split(diabetes, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
```

A random forest of 500 trees, as on Day 5. scikit-learn keeps a record of how
much each variable helped while it grows the trees; Part 2 reads it. A forest
is random, so fix `random_state`.

```{python}
rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=1)
rf = rf.fit(train[predictors], train["diabetes"])

test_prob = rf.predict_proba(test[predictors])[:, 1]    # probability of diabetes

round(roc_auc_score(test["diabetes"], test_prob), 3)
```

The test AUC is 0.794. This is the model we explain all day. R grows
different random trees, so its numbers differ slightly.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 2 — Impurity importance

**Impurity importance** adds up, for each variable, how much purer its splits
made the training rows, over all the trees. The forest works it out while it
is fitted, so it is free. scikit-learn stores it in
`feature_importances_`, one number per predictor, already scaled to add up
to 1.

```{python}
impurity_importance = pd.Series(rf.feature_importances_, index=predictors)
impurity_importance.sort_values(ascending=False).round(3)
```

Glucose has 0.318 of the total, then BMI 0.205, pedigree 0.198, age 0.169
and pregnancies 0.109. Glucose comes first by a long way.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 3 — Permutation importance

**Permutation importance** asks a different question: *how much worse is the
model on the test rows if one variable is scrambled?* Shuffle one column so
its values land on the wrong people, predict again, and see how much the AUC
drops. The model is not refitted.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
test_shuffled = test.copy()
test_shuffled["glucose"] = rng.permutation(test_shuffled[______].values)   # glucose now belongs to someone else

shuffled_prob = rf.predict_proba(______[predictors])[:, 1]
round(roc_auc_score(test_shuffled["diabetes"], shuffled_prob), 3)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
`rng.permutation()` returns the same glucose values in a random order. Then
predict on the shuffled test rows, `test_shuffled`.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
test_shuffled = test.copy()
test_shuffled["glucose"] = rng.permutation(test_shuffled["glucose"].values)

shuffled_prob = rf.predict_proba(test_shuffled[predictors])[:, 1]
round(roc_auc_score(test_shuffled["diabetes"], shuffled_prob), 3)
```

With glucose shuffled the AUC falls from 0.794 to 0.622, a drop of 0.172.
Run it with another seed and the drop changes a little.
:::
:::

One shuffle is one random draw, so in Part 4 we repeat it 20 times for each
variable and take the average drop.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 4 — A control: a column of pure noise

Which measure should we believe? Test both on something whose answer we
already know: [`data/diabetes_noise.csv`](data/diabetes_noise.csv) is the same
file with one more column, `noise`: random numbers unrelated to anything. Its
true importance is **zero**.

Read it, keep `noise` as a sixth predictor, and split it exactly as before.
The same `random_state` gives the same people in the test set.

```{python}
diabetes_noise = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes_noise.csv")
diabetes_noise["diabetes"] = (diabetes_noise["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)

predictors_noise = predictors + ["noise"]

train_noise, test_noise = train_test_split(diabetes_noise, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
```

Fit the same forest on these training rows and look at its impurity
importance.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
rf_noise = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=1)
rf_noise = rf_noise.fit(train_noise[______], train_noise["diabetes"])

pd.Series(rf_noise.feature_importances_, index=predictors_noise).sort_values(ascending=False).round(3)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The forest now uses all six predictors, `predictors_noise`.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
rf_noise = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=1)
rf_noise = rf_noise.fit(train_noise[predictors_noise], train_noise["diabetes"])

pd.Series(rf_noise.feature_importances_, index=predictors_noise).sort_values(ascending=False).round(3)
```

`noise` gets 0.154 of the total, level with the pedigree function (0.154),
and ahead of age (0.140) and pregnancies (0.104). By this measure, random
numbers are a respectable predictor.
:::
:::

Now the permutation importance of the same forest on the test rows.
`permutation_importance()` does what you did in Part 3, 20 times for each of
the six variables, with `scoring="roc_auc"`.

```{python}
perm = permutation_importance(rf_noise, test_noise[predictors_noise],
                              test_noise["diabetes"], scoring="roc_auc",
                              n_repeats=20, random_state=1)

perm_importance = pd.DataFrame({"variable": predictors_noise,
                                "importance": perm.importances_mean,
                                "sd": perm.importances_std})
perm_importance = perm_importance.sort_values("importance", ascending=False)
perm_importance.round(3)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
ordered = perm_importance.sort_values("importance")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.barh(ordered["variable"], ordered["importance"], xerr=ordered["sd"],
        color="coral", capsize=3)
ax.axvline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("Mean drop in test AUC when the variable is shuffled (± 1 SD)")
ax.set_title("Random forest: permutation importance")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

`noise` comes out at −0.005, with a standard deviation of 0.008: zero, as it
should. Glucose (0.150), BMI (0.031) and age (0.029) clearly beat it.
Pregnancies (0.012) and the pedigree function (0.006) are within about one
standard deviation of it.

Why the difference? Deep trees always find *some* split on a column with many
different values that tidies up a few training rows. Impurity importance
counts that; permutation importance on new people does not. So a variable that
does not clearly beat `noise` should not be called important.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key points
- Impurity importance is free and quick, but it is computed on the training rows and is biased: it gave pure noise 15% of the total.
- Permutation importance is the drop in test AUC when one column is shuffled. Repeat the shuffle and report the mean and spread.
- A noise column is a control: its true importance is zero, and permutation importance puts it there.
:::

::::::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Teaching choice.** Part 3 is the core: let students shuffle glucose by
hand before showing the loop or `permutation_importance()`. In Part 4 ask the
room, before running the cells, where they expect `noise` to land in each
ranking.

**Expected values.** Data: 750 rows, split 80/20 with seed 42. R: training
600 (218 pos), test 150 (55 pos). Python: training 600 (216 pos), test 150
(57 pos). `diabetes_noise.csv` gives the same test people as
`diabetes_clean.csv` in each language (checked). Forest test AUC: R 0.753,
Python 0.794. Impurity shares, R: glucose 0.373, mass 0.182, age 0.164,
pedigree 0.162, pregnant 0.119 (raw 80.2, 39.2, 35.2, 34.7, 25.5). Python:
glucose 0.318, mass 0.205, pedigree 0.198, age 0.169, pregnant 0.109. One
shuffle of glucose (seed 1): R AUC 0.578, drop 0.175; Python 0.622, drop
0.172. Noise forest test AUC: R 0.760, Python 0.789. Impurity shares with
noise, R: glucose 0.337, mass 0.156, age 0.141, **noise 0.130**, pedigree
0.127, pregnant 0.109. Python: glucose 0.283, mass 0.165, **noise 0.154**,
pedigree 0.154, age 0.140, pregnant 0.104. Permutation importance (20
repeats, mean (SD)), R: glucose 0.129 (0.039), mass 0.028 (0.008), pedigree
0.011 (0.009), **noise 0.0004 (0.009)**, age −0.002 (0.013), pregnant −0.006
(0.015). Python: glucose 0.150 (0.041), mass 0.031 (0.019), age 0.029
(0.016), pregnant 0.012 (0.021), pedigree 0.006 (0.008), **noise −0.005
(0.008)**. The two forests disagree on age; only glucose and BMI are clearly
above noise in both.

**Common failures.** (1) Omitting `event_level = "second"` in R: every AUC
becomes 1 − AUC and the drops change sign. (2) Shuffling the training rows
instead of the test rows, which flatters every variable the forest overfitted.
(3) Reading one shuffle as the importance. (4) In R, forgetting `set.seed(1)`
before the fit, so the numbers move on every run. (5) Comparing raw ranger
importances (80.2, 39.2, ...) with scikit-learn's shares.

**Timing.** Part 1 ten minutes, Part 2 ten, Part 3 fifteen, Part 4 twenty-five.
:::
